posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
Would it be possible to make a plate that contains colloidal silver by mixing gelatin with AgNO3 and then exposing to uv light?

In that case subsequent dipping in a re-halogenating bleach might convert those mini colloidal silver crystals to ultra fine AgBr crystals, yes?

So, we would have a system where the uv-exposure time would determine the size of the final halide crystals. After that sensitization could take place in a bath with pinacyanol dye.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** Would it be possible to make a plate that contains colloidal silver by mixing gelatin with AgNO3 and then exposing to uv light?

I don't see why you'd want to expose the plate to UV light.

You can directly reduce the AgNO3 to form colloidal silver, which then can be bleached in a rehalogenating bleach. You can spectrally sensitize such an emulsion. If you search the forum for LEROY (see also the Leroy paper in the Lippmann section) you'll find a couple of posts on that. 

> In that case subsequent dipping in a re-halogenating bleach might convert those mini colloidal silver crystals to ultra fine AgBr crystals, yes?

Yes. I've made a few holograms on such emulsions. They didn't come out nearly as bright as the ones recorded on “normal” silver halide emulsions. One of the main problem is noise – maybe grain growth also.

posts.content_md:
Maybe an additional UV activated reducing agent would help, as here described:

Might be tricky to get this to work in a gelatin emulsion...

J. Phys. Chem. C, 111 (14), 5300 -5308, 2007. 10.1021/jp067010s S1932-7447(06)07010-5

Web Release Date: March 17, 2007

Copyright © 2007 American Chemical Society

Facile Size-Controlled Synthesis of Silver Nanoparticles in UV-Irradiated Tungstosilicate Acid Solution

Liangbao Yang, Yuhua Shen,* Anjian Xie,* and Baocheng Zhang

School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Anhui University, Hefei 230039, P. R. China, and State Key Laboratory of Coordination Chemistry, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210093, P. R. China

Received: October 25, 2006

In Final Form: January 30, 2007

Abstract:

A method for size-controlled synthesis of silver nanocomplex is proposed and described. The synthesis is based on the reduction of silver nitrate (AgNO3) by a UV-irradiated arginine (Arg)-tungstosilicate acid (TSA, H4SiW12O40) solution. The method allows synthesis of spherical particles of diameter between several nanometers and several hundreds of nanometers by varying the molar ratio of silver nitrate to TSA, the pH of the reaction solution, and the reaction temperature. The formation of the Arg complexed with TSA ions is demonstrated. The experimental results show that Arg-TSA colloidal particles are a new kind of organic-inorganic template for the synthesis of organized assemblies of silver nanocomplex, wherein the Arg-TSA complex acts as a UV-switchable reducing agent for silver ion. The conductance of the Arg-TSA solution was measured as a function of reaction time. The nanoparticles were characterized by ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction analysis, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, electron diffraction, and transmission electron microscopy and by use of a Zetasizer instrument.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Tom B.:** Maybe an additional UV activated reducing agent would help

The crux of colloidal silver formation seems to be – not unlike “regular” silver halide formation – high silver concentration and small particle size are difficult to match at the same time.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I read that silver nitrate reacts with organic material when illuminated with UV. Would the gelatin not provide the necessary organic material? Or how about adding some sugar to the emulsion.

The idea is to coat the plate first with a mix of AgNO3 and gelatin and then create the colloidal silver after the plate has been coated. That way there will be not much movement of AgNO3 in the plate while the silver crystals form.

Yes, that's what I tried also with a couple of different sugars. I equally tried hydroquinone, metol and ascorbic acid. And some day, I am going to give sodium borohydride a chance. 

The key problem with all those agents seems to be how to get a uniform layer.
